items.title: Lean and Mathlib maintainers certify a machine-checked proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
items.why: A week ago this would have been the setup for a joke. Instead the Lean community has put its name to a statement that a 17-million-line formal proof of the Riemann Hypothesis checks out, statement and all, and the mathematical web is having the best kind of weekend. Worth noticing how much of the statement is about process: what exactly was verified, against which criteria, and by whom.
items.summary: Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library on November 20, depending only on Mathlib. Members of the Lean and Mathlib communities spent the following day checking it and have issued a joint statement certifying that both the formal statement of the conjecture and its proof are correct.

items.title: Webb catches the aftermath of one star swallowing another in Andromeda
items.why: Stellar mergers are usually something you infer after the fact from a strange leftover. Here astronomers caught one in a neighbouring galaxy and had Webb looking within seven weeks, which in this business counts as rushing to the scene. The infrared view of the debris is where the new detail lives.
items.summary: In the Andromeda galaxy, a small star spiralled into a giant companion some 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, setting off a violent eruption. The James Webb Space Telescope observed the scene 47 days later, giving astronomers a close look at how two stars combine into one.

items.title: The rise and fall of IBM's System/4 Pi, the computers that flew the Space Shuttle
items.why: Flight software has to run on something, and for the Shuttle that something was a family of IBM aerospace machines with a wonderfully grandiose name. Ken Shirriff traces the line from its origins to the AP-101B units in the avionics bay, with the usual photos of real hardware. Read it for the redundancy story: four computers voting, and a fifth waiting in case they all agreed on the wrong thing.
items.summary: An illustrated history of IBM's System/4 Pi family of aerospace computers, built around the AP-101B models that controlled the Space Shuttle from its first launch in 1981. The piece covers how the family came about, where else it flew, and why it eventually faded out.

items.title: Lundy, the Bristol Channel island where seabirds came back and fishermen helped draw the lines
items.why: Conservation stories tend to come in two flavours, fences or failure, so a third one is welcome. Lundy got its seabirds back over decades while keeping a working fishing community, and the fishermen were in the room when the UK's first no-take zone was drawn. A short video piece, calm and hopeful.
items.summary: Mongabay's video team visits Lundy, a rugged island between Wales and England, where decades of conservation work have brought back thousands of seabirds and revived the marine life around it. Local fishermen helped design the marine protected area, including the UK's first no-take zone, and the island now supports wildlife, fishing and visitors together.

items.title: Mrs. Moreau's Warbler: Stephen Moss on how birds got their names
items.why: Every birder eventually wonders who all these people in the field guide were and why a perfectly good warbler is named after somebody's wife. Stephen Moss wrote a whole book about it, and 10,000 Birds has dusted off its review. Good reading for anyone who has ever had to explain a megapode named after an explorer.
items.summary: A review, republished from the 10,000 Birds archive, of Stephen Moss's book on the origins of bird names. The reviewer finds it takes a different approach from earlier books on the subject, looking at the people, places and habits behind the names birds carry.

items.title: A website keeps Boston's lost bars open, at least in memory
items.why: Every city has bars that live on mainly in the arguments of people who drank there. Someone in Boston has given them a permanent home on the web, which is a public service of sorts. Expect a lot of 'wait, that's where that was'.
items.summary: Universal Hub points to a website devoted to remembering Boston bars that have closed for good, an online memorial for the city's vanished watering holes.

items.title: Split-level I/O scheduling: hooking the system call, page cache and block layers at once, via The Morning Paper
items.why: The block layer knows where the bytes go but not who asked for them; the syscall layer knows who asked but not where they go. This SOSP paper's answer is to stop picking sides and hang scheduler hooks at both ends plus the page cache in between. Adrian Colyer's write-up is a good refresher on why write accounting through the page cache is so slippery.
items.summary: A Morning Paper review of split-level I/O scheduling, a framework that lets a scheduler see I/O at the system-call, page-cache and block levels. With that combined view it can reorder writes and attribute I/O to its true source accurately, which neither block-level nor syscall-level schedulers manage alone.

items.title: Valkey swaps the sorted-set skiplist for a high-fanout B+ tree and saves a lot of memory
items.why: The skiplist has been the sorted set's backbone since the Redis days, beloved for being easy to get right and not so beloved for its pointer overhead. Valkey 9.2 replaces it with a cache-friendly B+ tree variant and shows its working: SIMD searches, linked leaves, fast paths for sequential inserts. A proper data-structures deep dive.
items.summary: Valkey 9.2 replaces the skiplist behind large sorted sets with fbtree, a high-fanout B+ tree tuned for its workload and memory allocator. In a test with five million members, per-member overhead fell by 36 to 43 percent, and the post explains why the change was made and how the new structure works.

items.title: Worthless idiot, donkey head: the pompous pedant as a stock joke of the Renaissance stage
items.why: The know-it-all who corrects your Latin is not an internet invention; Italian comedy was mocking him five centuries ago. Arnoud Visser looks at what the stage pedant was really a jab at, namely humanist learning and its airs. A reassuring reminder that the reply guy has a long and well-documented lineage.
items.summary: An essay by Arnoud Visser on the pedant, a stock comic character of the Italian Renaissance stage. It looks at how the figure was tied to ideas of intellectual superiority and social standing, and how the satire targeted the erudition and lofty ideals of humanist scholars.

items.title: Folk Alley's Thanksgiving show: songs of gratitude, family awkwardness, and a full set about corn
items.why: Holiday radio specials can be treacly, so credit to Folk Alley for admitting that Thanksgiving also comes with weird feelings and then devoting an entire set to corn. A good companion for a quiet Sunday, even from the other side of the world where nobody is basting anything.
items.summary: This week's Folk Alley Radio Show is a Thanksgiving special, mixing songs about the holiday, songs about gratitude and songs about the mixed feelings the day can bring, plus a whole set of songs about corn. The show airs on public and community radio stations across the US.

items.title: A 28-million-year-old dolphin from South Carolina had serrated, steak-knife teeth
items.why: Not a dinosaur, but palaeontology news with teeth, literally. Serrations are the sort of thing you expect on a T. rex or a shark, so finding them in a toothed whale for the first time is a tidy bit of convergent evolution. The Ashley Formation keeps proving that the Charleston area was a rough neighbourhood in the Oligocene.
items.summary: Researchers have described a new species of the early toothed whale Ankylorhiza from roughly 28-million-year-old rocks near Charleston. Its teeth carry serrated edges, a feature never seen before in a toothed whale, which points to a predator that sliced up large prey.

items.title: BepiColombo's X-ray telescope wakes up after eight years on the road to Mercury
items.why: Eight years and ten billion kilometres is a long time to keep an instrument switched off and hope it still works. This one apparently came out of the box better than its builders expected, which is the rarest phrase in spaceflight. Mercury's surface chemistry has been a tease since MESSENGER, so this is worth watching.
items.summary: An X-ray instrument aboard the European-Japanese mission heading for Mercury has made its first observations of cosmic sources, and it is performing beyond expectations. Once in orbit it will map the X-rays given off by Mercury's surface, which should reveal what the planet is made of and help explain how it formed.

items.title: A short tail in a photograph may mark a new langur species in the mountains of Laos
items.why: Our wildcard, from Penang's own neighbourhood of limestone karst and elusive primates. Describing a species from photos alone is a bold move and the piece is fair about the controversy. Still, the Annamites are the range that gave us the saola, so nobody should be too surprised when they hide one more.
items.summary: Scientists have proposed a new species, the short-tailed langur, based on camera images from the Annamite Mountains of Laos showing a monkey whose tail is markedly shorter than its limestone-dwelling relatives. There is no specimen or DNA yet, and other primatologists want genetic evidence before accepting it.

items.title: A miscellany of sparrows, the world's most familiar and least looked-at birds
items.why: Every birder walks past House Sparrows on the way to something rarer, including in Penang, where they share the shophouses with Eurasian Tree Sparrows. This is a pleasant ramble through the wider family, from Italian hybrids to desert specialists. It might just make the next one on the five-foot way worth a second look.
items.summary: A tour of the true sparrows, starting with the House Sparrow's spread out of North Africa across Europe and Asia and, with human help, much of the rest of the world. It then looks at less familiar relatives such as the Spanish, Italian, Cape and Desert Sparrows, illustrated with the author's own photographs.

items.title: Green River Festival announces the first wave of its 2027 lineup
items.why: It's November and western Massachusetts is already planning June. Green River in Greenfield is one of New England's friendliest festivals, and the first wave leans indie with a healthy streak of roots music running through it. Worth bookmarking in case a favourite or two gets added in the next round.
items.summary: The Green River Festival in Greenfield, Massachusetts, has named the first artists for its June 2027 edition, with Big Thief, Death Cab for Cutie and Remi Wolf at the top. The undercard mixes indie rock, folk and Americana acts including Sylvan Esso, Julia Jacklin, Jess Williamson and Nick Shoulders.

items.title: Amazing Stories, the first science fiction magazine, turns 100 with an anniversary issue
items.why: Hugo Gernsback launched Amazing Stories in 1926 and more or less invented the genre's commercial life, along with the word scientifiction, mercifully retired. A centenary issue is a nice moment, made bittersweet by the tribute to the publisher who brought it back. The rest of the scroll is the usual grab-bag of fannish news.
items.summary: File 770's daily roundup leads with the Fall 2026 issue of Amazing Stories, which marks the magazine's 100th anniversary with new fiction and a tribute to the late Steve Davidson, who revived the title. The rest of the roundup covers auctions, art and other news from fandom.

items.title: City Island Nautical Museum, a seafaring village's memory in the Bronx
items.why: City Island is the part of New York that looks like it wandered down from coastal Maine and decided to stay. As the boatyards turned into condos, the museum ended up holding the island's shipbuilding past, from yacht builders to the sailmakers. A good excuse to take the bus to the end of the line.
items.summary: City Island, joined to the rest of the Bronx by a short causeway, was once a busy boatbuilding and yachting centre, and most of its yards have since given way to housing. The local nautical museum, in an old schoolhouse, collects the models, photographs and artefacts of that maritime past.

items.title: Infographics from a 1920s Turkish law journal, drawn as the republic remade itself
items.why: Information design from a country rebuilding its legal system from scratch in real time. These covers turn statistics and court structures into charts and diagrams that look surprisingly modern. A reminder that the visual explainer is a lot older than the slide deck.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review gathers covers from a Turkish justice gazette published in the mid-1920s, just after the founding of the republic. The covers present legal statistics and the workings of the new courts as bold charts and diagrams, mirroring a country in the middle of sweeping legal reform.

items.title: Marc Brooker on how Aurora DSQL tries to make simple architectures the default
items.why: Brooker's argument is that most of the complexity in database-backed systems is accidental, and that the database should soak it up rather than push it onto every application. Read it as a designer's rationale rather than a brochure: the interesting part is which hard problems he chose to move below the line.
items.summary: Marc Brooker walks through the design choices behind Aurora DSQL, a distributed relational database, and how features like serverless scaling, multi-region availability and optimistic concurrency are meant to spare developers from building caching, sharding and failover layers of their own.

items.title: Polydraw: a peer-to-peer drawing game built in Scheme for the Lisp Game Jam
items.why: A small team, a tight deadline, a Lisp dialect compiled to WebAssembly, and a party game where you may only draw in triangles. This is exactly the late-90s spirit: people building something silly and clever for the fun of it, then writing up the daily devlog so you can follow along.
items.summary: Spritely's entry in the autumn Lisp Game Jam is Polydraw, a guess-the-drawing party game played peer to peer, in which the artist has a minute and can use only triangles. The post is a day-by-day devlog of building it with the Goblins distributed-objects library and the Hoot Scheme-to-WebAssembly compiler.

items.title: Sand dunes on other worlds turn out to record how hard the wind blows, not just which way
items.why: Planetary scientists have read wind direction off dune shapes for decades, but speed was the missing half of the forecast. Stanford's trick of working it out from grain size is the kind of quietly clever physics that turns old orbital photos into new data. Mars, Titan and friends just got anemometers nobody had to launch.
items.summary: A new paper in PNAS argues that the size of the sand grains in a dune field can be used to estimate how fast the wind moves over it. That would let researchers squeeze wind speeds, not only directions, out of existing orbital images of worlds with atmospheres.

items.title: Two mountain-building spurts may have set up Earth's great oxygen boosts
items.why: Geology as a life-support system: more mountain means more rock to weather, more nutrients washing into the sea, and eventually more oxygen to breathe. The neat part is the timing, with two growth spurts lining up just ahead of two oxygenation events. A pleasing reminder that the planet's plumbing shaped its biology.
items.summary: Researchers identify two ancient periods when Earth's mountains grew taller, each shortly before one of the planet's major rises in oxygen. Their argument is that taller ranges sped up weathering, fed nutrients to the oceans and helped make room for complex life.

items.title: The Dusky Megapode, a mound-building bird from Raja Ampat, and the explorer it was named for
items.why: Megapodes skip the whole sitting-on-eggs business and let warm earth incubate them, which is about as practical as ornithology gets. This one lives on our side of the world, in eastern Indonesia, and the spotlight comes with a fine bit of naming history, including a ship's captain's wife who sailed in disguise. Fresh photos from Raja Ampat, too.
items.summary: A 10,000 Birds species profile of the Dusky Megapode, photographed in Raja Ampat, Indonesia. It covers the bird and the story behind its scientific name, which honours the French naval officer and cartographer Louis de Freycinet, whose wife Rose famously joined his 1817 voyage dressed as a sailor.

items.title: Boston's Swan Boats get a restoration ahead of their 150th season
items.why: The Swan Boats have been pedalling round the Public Garden lagoon since 1877, which makes next year the big one-five-oh. The century-old swans are getting fixed up and will go on display, a rare chance to see them out of the water. Pure Make Way for Ducklings territory.
items.summary: The wooden swans that front the Public Garden's pedal-powered boats are being restored before the attraction's 150th anniversary season. The century-old figures are set to be shown off in Boston as part of the celebrations.

items.title: Jim Kweskin, 86, goes back to the songsters on a new roots album
items.why: Kweskin's Jug Band was a fixture of the early-60s Cambridge folk scene, so this is the Club Passim lineage still making records. At 86 he's leaning into the songster tradition, the travelling musicians who played whatever the crowd wanted after the Civil War. No Depression says the fingerpicking hasn't aged a day.
items.summary: No Depression reviews A Songster's Journey, a new album from jug band veteran Jim Kweskin, who first recorded in 1963. The record draws on the songster tradition of itinerant players who mixed genres freely, and the reviewer praises his easy, flowing guitar work.

items.title: Alta's rock carvings: seven thousand years of reindeer, boats and bears in Norway's far north
items.why: Not replicas behind glass but the real thing, cut straight into the bedrock above the Arctic Circle. The clever bit is the geology: as the land rose after the Ice Age, each generation carved closer to the new shoreline, so the walk is also a timeline. Worth the trip to Finnmark on its own.
items.summary: Alta Museum's outdoor site in northern Norway holds thousands of prehistoric carvings, some more than 7,000 years old, showing animals, boats, hunts and rituals. Because the coast rose after the last Ice Age, carvings made at different times sit at different heights.

items.title: Proving etcd's and HashiCorp's Raft libraries safe, one model refinement at a time
items.why: Two production Raft libraries, same paper, rather different code, and the interesting stuff is in the gaps: pre-votes, snapshots, leadership transfer and etcd's deliberate departures on membership change. Antithesis loops model checking, trace-validated testing and TLA+ proofs until the model and the code agree. The bugs each step shook out are the real read.
items.summary: Antithesis and Hillel Wayne describe modelling the etcd and HashiCorp Raft implementations in TLA+, validating the models against real execution traces, and iterating until core safety properties could be proved. Along the way the process exposed bugs in the code and gaps in the models, which they fixed.

items.title: Gutting a FireWire audio interface and giving it a USB-C brain
items.why: A perfectly good eight-in, eight-out interface condemned by its connector is a familiar tragedy. Rather than an adapter, this hack rips out the FireWire controller and wires an XMOS USB audio board into the original converters, with careful signal routing to keep jitter down. Open files and a plan to rescue other orphaned boxes make it a proper community project.
items.summary: A hacker replaced the FireWire controller in a PreSonus FireStudio Project with an XMOS-based USB audio board, reusing the original analogue circuitry. The design files are public, and the project aims to extend the approach to other FireWire-era interfaces.

items.title: Two Italian aristocrats and their competing Moorish fantasy castles
items.why: Nineteenth-century Italy produced two noblemen who independently decided that what Tuscany and Emilia needed was the Alhambra, turned up to eleven. One built his for electrohomeopathic healing, which is a sentence. The Public Domain Review's tour through the old images is gloriously over the top.
items.summary: An essay on Rocchetta Mattei and Castello di Sammezzano, two lavish Moorish Revival castles built by eccentric aristocrats in mid-19th-century Italy. It explores their kaleidoscopic interiors and the odd ideas, from quack medicine to orientalist fantasy, behind them.

items.title: Slag from an English coast is turning into brand-new rock within a human lifetime
items.why: Geologists found sedimentary rock on a beach that used to be sand, made of fragments from a nearby slag heap and dated by the rubbish caught inside it, coin included. Geology is meant to be slow; this is the fast-forward version. BLDGBLOG riffs on what accelerated landscapes mean.
items.summary: BLDGBLOG looks at a study of new sedimentary rock forming on the English coast from industrial slag. Trash embedded in the layers shows some of it formed within the last few decades, a striking case of human industry speeding up geology.

items.title: Boston's CITGO sign is relit over Kenmore Square, a little higher and a little to the east
items.why: Nur sent this one in, and it is hard to argue: the sign has been the unofficial beacon for every Fenway walk home since the sixties, and it survived years of preservation fights to get here. Relocating a landmark thirty feet up and a hundred and twenty feet over is the sort of thing only Boston would turn into a party, complete with a pep band and, inevitably, Sweet Caroline.
items.summary: After months off the skyline for restoration, the red-and-blue CITGO triangle in Kenmore Square was switched back on on 19 November. As part of a redevelopment of the square it now sits about thirty feet higher and roughly a hundred and twenty feet east of its old perch, and the relighting came with a public countdown and live music on the Commonwealth Avenue Mall.

items.title: Aoife O'Donovan and Chris Thile bring their Wassail! holiday show to Santa Fe's Lensic
items.why: Favourite-artist rule applies, and gladly: O'Donovan and Thile go back to the Nickel Creek and Crooked Still era, and a winter tour of carols and wassail songs is the natural habitat for a voice like hers and a mandolin like his. Worth a look for the setlist hints even if Santa Fe is a long way from Penang.
items.summary: The Santa Fe New Mexican previews the Wassail! holiday tour from Aoife O'Donovan and Chris Thile, which stops at the Lensic Performing Arts Center in early December. The duo pair seasonal folk songs and carols with their own material in a stripped-back two-person show.

items.title: A triple star 28 light-years away that stellar-evolution models say shouldn't exist
items.why: Every so often the neighbourhood turns out to be weirder than the textbooks. The interesting bit is the common-envelope phase, where one star swallows its partner in its own outer layers, which usually wrecks any third companion; this one apparently kept all three, which is either a lucky orbit or a hole in the theory.
items.summary: Astronomers report a nearby triple-star system whose current arrangement is hard to square with how close binaries are thought to evolve through a shared-envelope stage. Its survival suggests that such episodes may be gentler, or more varied, than standard models allow.

items.title: Sound waves from sunspots launch the Sun's spiky plasma jets
items.why: The coronal heating problem is the astrophysics equivalent of a bug that only shows up in production: the outside of the Sun is far hotter than the surface, and nobody can fully say why. Tracking a couple of hundred of these jets back to acoustic waves leaking out of sunspots is one more careful log line in a very long debugging session.
items.summary: A study in The Astrophysical Journal follows around two hundred dynamic fibrils, short jets of plasma that shoot up from the solar surface, and links them to sound waves rising from sunspots. The jets are one candidate for carrying energy into the corona, the outer atmosphere that is hundreds of times hotter than the surface below.

items.title: Sharing thermals with the griffon vultures of the Baronnies, from a paraglider
items.why: Most bird photography involves a hide and a lot of patience; this involves a harness, a wing and a sky full of two-metre scavengers who could not care less that you are there. A raptor fan will appreciate the view from the inside of a thermal, and the reintroduction story behind why there are vultures in Provence at all.
items.summary: A photographer and paraglider pilot from Vaison-la-Romaine writes about years of flying alongside the griffon vultures of the Baronnies in Provence, and later photographing them from the cliffs. It is a first-person account of how the birds use rising air and how they react to a human sharing it.

items.title: Visulahti, the Finnish wax museum beloved for how bad its figures are
items.why: There is a particular joy in a place that set out to be impressive and became famous for the opposite. This one has a cult following in Finland precisely because its celebrities look slightly wrong, and because nobody has updated the line-up since the TV stars stopped being famous.
items.summary: The Visulahti Wax Museum near Mikkeli opened in 1983 with earnest ambitions, but its rarely refreshed and often unflattering figures have turned it into a nostalgic, faintly eerie attraction. Visitors now come mostly for the awkwardness and the period charm.

items.title: Virtual consensus in Delos: building a log you can swap out from under itself, via The Morning Paper
items.why: Brooks told us to plan to throw one away; the Delos team took it literally and built the throwing-away into the architecture. The virtual log abstraction, with sealable loglets that can be replaced while the system runs, is a neat answer to having to ship on someone else's consensus while keeping the option to write your own.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer's write-up of an OSDI 2020 paper on Delos, a table store built for control-plane services that needed strong durability and consistency on a short deadline. Its key idea is a virtualised shared log that lets the underlying consensus implementation be changed later without taking the service down.

items.title: Open firmware turns e-paper supermarket price tags into tiny picture frames
items.why: Electronic shelf labels are a lot of radio and display hardware deployed to show a number, which makes them perfect fodder for repurposing. A small open firmware project gives them Bluetooth image uploads from a browser and a slideshow mode, in four colours no less.
items.summary: The pin16 project is open firmware for two models of Solum e-paper shelf labels, letting them receive images over Bluetooth from a web page and cycle through them as a slideshow. Installing it needs a one-time SWD flash and wipes the factory firmware, so it is for tags you own.

items.title: Irish families who said their grandmother was a seal
items.why: This is the sort of piece the Ireland category exists for: not a place to visit but a belief that lived in families along the coast, where a selkie ancestor explained a webbed hand or a pull toward the sea. The essay digs into the darker side of the old tales, which are often about capture and loss rather than romance.
items.summary: An Aeon essay by Jordan Lee Borgman on the Irish folk tradition of families tracing their descent to selkies, seals who could shed their skins and live as humans. It reads those stories as a record of how coastal communities thought about kinship with animals, and the grief and coercion woven into them.

items.title: Jean-Michel Jarre on how Oxygène was made
items.why: In 1976 an unknown 28-year-old made an all-synthesizer instrumental album in a home studio and it went on to sell something like twenty million copies. The wildcard pick for the gear-minded: Jarre talks about treating sound itself as the material, not just the notes, which is the whole electronic-music idea in one sentence.
items.summary: Jean-Michel Jarre tells the story of recording Oxygène, his six-part 1976 synthesizer album, from his late-sixties restlessness with genre boundaries to the instruments and techniques he used. The piece also covers its recent remix for Dolby Atmos.

items.title: The typists, editors and spouses who quietly shaped modern literature
items.why: Behind a lot of famous prose is somebody else's typewriter. The essay is a good reminder that Henry James dictated to Theodora Bosanquet and that Véra Nabokov did far more than file the carbons, and it pairs nicely with the archive angle: much of what we know about these books survives because those women kept the drafts.
items.summary: Christine Jacobson's essay looks at literary amanuenses such as Theodora Bosanquet, Véra Nabokov and Valerie Eliot, who took dictation, typed and revised manuscripts and championed the work, often with little pay or credit. It argues their labour was central to how several modern classics came to exist.

items.title: 2026 ED138, a big icy world beyond Pluto, may be the sixth dwarf planet
items.why: Somewhere a planetarium gift shop is quietly panicking about its posters. The fun part is where it hid: in one of the most star-crowded stretches of sky, where faint moving dots are easy to lose among the background, which suggests the outer solar system still has room for surprises bigger than a rounding error.
items.summary: Astronomers report a large, distant, icy body beyond Pluto, catalogued as 2026 ED138, that went unnoticed for years because it sits against a very dense star field. If its size holds up, it could join the short official list of dwarf planets and hint that more such worlds are waiting farther out.

items.title: Radio telescopes pin down a binary of two hot-tempered red dwarfs
items.why: Red dwarfs are the galaxy's most common stars and its most cantankerous, and knowing their masses precisely matters for anyone hoping their planets are habitable. The catch here is the rarer of the pair, an oddball class of rapidly spinning, strangely varying red dwarf that nobody had weighed properly in a binary before.
items.summary: Using the continent-spanning Very Long Baseline Array, astronomers tracked a pair of flaring red dwarfs with enough precision to measure their orbit and properties. One of them is a so-called complex periodic variable, and this is the first time a star of that type has been measured accurately as part of a binary.

items.title: Nepal's crow festival, and the city sprawl testing the friendship
items.why: House crows are a familiar sight on Penang's own streets, so this one hits close to home. Kaag Tihar, the day in the Tihar festival when Nepalis put out food for crows as messengers, is a lovely tradition; the story is about what happens to that bond when the trees come down and the city's rubbish changes what crows eat and where they roost.
items.summary: Each year during Tihar, around Diwali, people in Nepal honour house crows with offerings. Mongabay reports that in Kathmandu, rapid urban growth, a steep loss of green space and the felling of thousands of roadside trees are pushing the birds into closer, more strained contact with residents.

items.title: The Promotions Gallery, where Paris mining students paint the catacombs
items.why: A yearbook, but underground and in paint. The old secret stairway from the School of Mines into the quarries is closed now, yet the quarry inspectorate still lets each new class descend and add its mural, which makes this a living tradition rather than a museum of graffiti.
items.summary: Beneath Paris, in the old quarry tunnels linked to the catacombs, students of the city's School of Mines keep up a tradition of painting a mural for each incoming class. The works are made around the feast of Saint Barbara, patron saint of miners, in early December, with official permission even though the students' private entrance is no longer used.

items.title: A wall of one hundred PC fans, built to make good on a boast
items.why: Pure late-90s energy: a project with no reason to exist except that someone said a thing out loud and then had to prove it. Watch for the daisy-chained splitters and the question of whether the wall actually moves the room.
items.summary: Sasa Karanovic claimed his homemade fan controller could drive a hundred fans, so he built an aluminium-extrusion frame holding exactly that many case fans, chained together through a pile of splitters. Hackaday enjoys it as a gloriously pointless piece of engineering.

items.title: Cracking open a ten-dollar round-screen badge and giving it an open SDK
items.why: This is the good stuff: buy a cheap gadget, find out it is more computer than it has any right to be, and turn it into something the community can program. The teardown-to-Ghidra-to-open-SDK arc is a tidy little template for anyone with a drawer of mystery electronics.
items.summary: A hacker called Sabas reverse engineered the JieLi AC707N, an inexpensive wearable badge with a round 360 by 360 touchscreen, Bluetooth LE and 4 MB of flash. By pulling apart the companion app and the firmware he worked out how to flash custom code onto sealed units and published an open SDK and firmware for it.

items.title: glibc weighs letting admins refuse to run binaries that can't do ASLR
items.why: A Node.js Brotli overflow turned out worse than it should have been because the official Linux builds couldn't use address space randomisation, and glibc's answer is a set of tunables to forbid such binaries outright. LWN's angle is the useful one: it is a sensible belt, but the trousers are still the memory-unsafe code underneath.
items.summary: LWN looks at proposed glibc tunables that would let administrators block programs built without support for address space layout randomisation. The idea was prompted by a buffer overflow in Node.js whose impact was worsened by how its binaries were linked, and the article weighs what the change would and would not fix.

items.title: Jevons, sunspots and the price of corn
items.why: In 1875 one of the founders of modern economics argued that trade cycles marched in step with the sunspot cycle, by way of the weather and the harvest. It didn't hold up, which is half the charm; the other half is that later researchers found sunshine does seem to nudge something in markets, just not the way he imagined.
items.summary: William Stanley Jevons proposed that harvests, grain prices and business cycles followed the roughly eleven-year sunspot period. Futility Closet recalls the theory, notes that it failed, and points to a 2001 study suggesting that sunny weather has a measurable effect on stock returns.

items.title: The Fall of the House of Usher, 1928: Poe as early American avant-garde film
items.why: Long before music videos borrowed the look, a couple of amateurs in Rochester made Poe out of tilted sets, prisms and shadows. It's only a short film and it's in the public domain, so this is a perfect idle-moment watch: thirteen minutes of mood with no dialogue to keep up with.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review presents the 1928 silent short adaptation of Poe's story, made by James Sibley Watson and Melville Webber and counted among the first avant-garde films made in the United States. It tells the tale through distorted sets, multiple exposures and expressionist lighting rather than through plot.

items.title: A 309-million-year-old amphibian ancestor turns up in the Chicago swamps
items.why: Not a dinosaur, but the palaeontology slot will take a creature that predates them by some ninety million years. Carboniferous Illinois was a steaming coal swamp, and the Field Museum keeps pulling new residents out of it; this one fills in a branch of the family tree that eventually gave us frogs and salamanders.
items.summary: Field Museum researchers have identified a previously unrecognised species of early amphibian relative from roughly 309 million years ago, when the Chicago region was a hot, swampy coastal lowland. The animal sheds light on how the lineage leading to modern frogs and salamanders got started.

items.title: Spyrius, the six-set LEGO space theme from the 90s, gets a loving redux
items.why: Spyrius only ever had six sets, which makes it the deep cut of Classic Space nostalgia. Builder Edge of Bricks gives it the redux treatment: an octagonal base echoing the old canopy, a walker in the spirit of the Robo Guardian, and a reworked Saucer Scout with sharper angles. Bonus points for anyone who still has the printed tiles in a drawer somewhere.
items.summary: A new diorama revives LEGO's short-lived 1990s Spyrius theme with a base, a walker and a spacecraft, each nodding to specific original sets. It mixes classic printed parts and updated minifigures with modern building techniques.

items.title: Fermi's 14-year sky map starts filling in astronomy's MeV gap
items.why: Gamma-ray astronomy has long had an awkward blind spot around a few tens to hundreds of mega-electron volts, too high for one kind of detector and too low for another. Squeezing 14 years of Fermi data to see into it is the kind of patient instrument-wrangling that rarely makes headlines and deserves to.
items.summary: The Fermi Large Area Telescope collaboration has catalogued about 450 gamma-ray sources in the 20 to 200 MeV band, a range that is notoriously hard to observe. The result is the clearest all-sky view yet of low-energy gamma rays, published in the Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series.

items.title: Emergency-blanket plastic, stacked hundreds of layers deep, as insulation for Moon bases
items.why: The shiny blanket in every marathon finish line and first-aid kit turns out to be a decent starting point for lunar architecture. Stack enough layers and it shrugs off crushing loads while still keeping the heat where it belongs, which matters on a world that swings a few hundred degrees between day and night.
items.summary: Researchers built a multilayer insulation from the thin metallised film used in emergency blankets and found it keeps its thermal performance even under heavy compression. They suggest it could make sturdier, longer-lasting habitats for astronauts facing the Moon's temperature extremes.

items.title: Sarah Jarosz picks up Mountain Stage's Song of the Week
items.why: Favourite-artist rule applies, and gladly. Mountain Stage has been taping roots musicians in Charleston, West Virginia for decades, and a Jarosz set there is about as natural a fit as the show gets. A good one to put on while the Undercurrent anniversary tour is still rolling.
items.summary: West Virginia Public Broadcasting has chosen a Sarah Jarosz performance from the long-running radio show Mountain Stage as its weekly featured song, with a recording to listen to.

items.title: NetChain: a coordination service that lives in the switches, via The Morning Paper
items.why: An NSDI 2018 best paper that takes the ZooKeeper job and moves it out of the server chassis entirely, into programmable switches. Single-digit microsecond reads and writes are the headline; the interesting part is what it costs you in state size and failure handling when your replicas are network hardware.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer's write-up of NetChain, which implements a strongly consistent key-value coordination service on programmable switches using chain replication. It reports reads and writes around ten microseconds and very high throughput, and can be deployed incrementally in existing datacentres.

items.title: Dave Täht, the bufferbloat crusader, honoured with the Postel Award
items.why: The late Dave Täht spent years convincing standards bodies, router vendors and anyone within earshot that latency, not bandwidth, was what made the Internet feel broken. The fixes he championed went into Linux and into a lot of home routers you have probably used. A fitting tribute, and he reportedly wanted it partly so he could jam with a drummer who kept missing rehearsal.
items.summary: The Internet Society profiles Dave Täht as a recipient of its Jonathan B. Postel Service Award, recounting his long campaign against bufferbloat, the delay caused by data sitting in oversized network buffers, and his efforts to explain why low latency matters to everyday users.

items.title: Thunder Hole, the granite slot in Acadia that booms with the tide
items.why: Mount Desert Island's party trick: a glacier-cut channel with a small cavern at its end that compresses air on each incoming wave and lets go with a bang. Time it for a rising tide in rough weather, stand back, and enjoy one of New England's louder pieces of geology.
items.summary: Thunder Hole is a narrow inlet in the granite shoreline of Acadia National Park in Maine. When waves surge in near high tide they trap and compress air in a small undersea cavern, producing a thunderous boom and spray that can shoot many feet into the air.

items.title: Black oystercatchers and the rocky shore they cannot do without
items.why: A loud, red-billed shorebird with a very specific taste in real estate: the wave-splashed rocks between high and low tide. That fussiness is exactly what makes it a good gauge of how the Pacific coast is coping with rising seas and storms, and the Q&A explains why.
items.summary: Audubon California talks with Dan Orr about the black oystercatcher, which depends on the rocky intertidal zone from Alaska to Baja California, and about how climate change threatens that narrow strip of habitat.

items.title: Fifty thousand boat names, mapped and sorted
items.why: Boat owners are a nation of compulsive punsters, and someone finally put the evidence in one place. Expect a great many variations on Nauti, Reel and Seas the Day, plus the occasional Kessel Run for the nerds at the marina.
items.summary: A data visualisation project explores some fifty thousand registered boat names, grouping the recurring jokes, references and naming habits that turn up again and again.

items.title: A six-million-year-old pygmy sperm whale with the most lopsided face of any known mammal
items.why: Not a dinosaur, but the palaeontology slot rarely gets a skull this strange. The researchers first assumed the fossil had been squashed after death; it turns out the asymmetry was the design, which is the kind of plot twist fossils save for special occasions.
items.summary: Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct relative of today's pygmy sperm whales found in Peru, had a long downturned snout and a skull twisted so far to one side that it may be the most asymmetrical mammal on record. The team argues the odd shape helped it hunt prey along the seafloor.

items.title: Hera gets its first good close look at the asteroid DART hit four years ago
items.why: DART was a one-way shot with nobody left behind to inspect the dent, so this is the follow-up exam planetary defence has been waiting for. Worth noticing how much of the experiment's real answer, the change in Dimorphos's shape and orbit, depends on these pictures rather than the impact itself.
items.summary: ESA's Hera spacecraft has reached the Didymos and Dimorphos binary asteroid system and released some of the sharpest images of it since NASA's DART probe deliberately collided with the moonlet in 2022. Hera's job is to measure what the crash actually did.

items.title: Earth's air took on oxygen in three big pulses before the oceans caught up
items.why: The Great Oxidation Event gets taught as a single switch flipping; this revision says it was more of a stutter. A nice reminder that the planet's most important chemical makeover took its sweet time and didn't move in lockstep between sky and sea.
items.summary: New research proposes a revised timeline for how oxygen built up on early Earth, with the atmosphere going through three distinct rises while the oceans lagged behind. It refines the long-debated sequence of when and how the planet became breathable.

items.title: Čigoč, the Croatian village where storks outnumber the chimneys
items.why: A birder's village: white storks nesting on the roofs of old timber houses, with frog-filled wet meadows a short flap away. It was named Europe's first official Stork Village in the 1990s, and the arrangement between people and birds seems to work fine for both sides.
items.summary: Čigoč sits in Lonjsko Polje Nature Park beside an oxbow of the Sava River in Croatia. White storks build big nests on its traditional wooden houses and feed in the surrounding flooded meadows and pools, and the conservation group EuroNatur named it the first European Stork Village in 1994.

items.title: How Concord, Massachusetts, became the birthplace of the American pencil
items.why: Concord already has the Transcendentalists and the shot heard round the world, and it also gave America its wooden pencil. Readers of Walden will remember that the Thoreau family business was pencils, and Henry spent real effort improving them between bouts of philosophy.
items.summary: The first American-made wooden pencils came out of Concord in the early 1800s: graphite in a wooden casing, no eraser. A short history from the New England Historical Society on how the local industry got going and improved over time.

items.title: Christmas Bird Count data shows which Latin American and Caribbean birds are thriving
items.why: More than a century of volunteers standing in the cold with clipboards has turned into a real scientific dataset, and here it's pointed south of the US. The interesting part is the split: some species doing well, others quietly slipping, all of it from community counts.
items.summary: Audubon has used decades of Christmas Bird Count records to work out population trends for bird species across Latin America and the Caribbean, sorting those that are holding steady or growing from those that need conservation help.

items.title: Enlightening the I/O path: carrying request priority through the whole storage stack
items.why: A Morning Paper classic from FAST '17. Anyone who has watched a database checkpoint wreck tail latency under CFQ will nod along: setting an ionice class isn't enough when the page cache, filesystem journal and block layer all lose track of who is waiting on whom.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer walks through a paper on request-centric I/O prioritization, which tags foreground requests as critical and propagates that priority through caching, filesystem, block and device layers, while also resolving priority inversions where urgent I/O ends up waiting on background work. Tests with MongoDB and other databases show much steadier latency.

items.title: A little browser app that lays out eight-page fold-up zines from one sheet of paper
items.why: This is the small-tools-for-joy spirit in its purest form: someone gives zines to friends, got tired of rotating half the pages upside down by hand, and built the fix. Everything stays in the browser, and the latest update rearranges the editor to match how the booklet actually folds.
items.summary: The author makes eight-page zines from a single folded and cut A4 sheet and built a web app that lets you design each page the right way up, then exports a print-ready PDF with the panels arranged and rotated correctly. A new version groups pages into real spreads and adds a spread view.

items.title: Cabinets of curiosities, the jumbled ancestors of the modern museum
items.why: Nautilus shells, clockwork automata and narwhal tusks sold as unicorn horns, all crammed into one room as a picture of the known world. A short video essay on how these eccentric private collections turned into public museums, a fine idle-moment watch.
items.summary: An Aeon video on the Wunderkammer, the cabinet of wonders that wealthy collectors in early modern Europe filled with natural specimens, mechanical marvels and exotic objects, and how those collections paved the way for museums as we know them.

items.title: Why the flying car became science fiction's favourite symbol of progress
items.why: Every decade the flying car is promised and every decade it stays loud, expensive and slightly terrifying. Reactor asks why the genre keeps reaching for it anyway, which turns out to be a question about what we think the future should feel like more than what it should do.
items.summary: An essay tracing how the flying car became shorthand for the future across science fiction, despite being impractical and dangerous, and what its staying power says about how stories imagine progress.

items.title: Telluride Bluegrass lines up Punch Brothers, Sam Bush and Del McCoury for its next festival
items.why: Punch Brothers have been everywhere this autumn, and now they are booked for the summer too, in the one Colorado valley that has hosted more bluegrass history than seems physically possible. Sam Bush, the festival's unofficial mayor, is back as well, as is Del McCoury. The rest of the bill wanders well past string bands, which is very Telluride.
items.summary: Jambands.com reports the first lineup for the next Telluride Bluegrass Festival. Among the acts named are Punch Brothers, the Sam Bush Band, the Del McCoury Band, Yonder Mountain String Band, Caamp, Stephen Wilson Jr. and The War on Drugs.

items.title: Radie Peat of Lankum goes solo with old ballads that still have teeth
items.why: Lankum made Irish traditional song feel heavy and dangerous again, and their singer's first solo record seems to keep going in that direction. The review's point is a good one: these ballads get filed as quaint, but they are mostly about violence, longing and indifferent skies. Worth a listen for the voice alone, which apparently does without any classical polish.
items.summary: Folk Alley reviews 'No Human Tongue Can Tell', the debut solo album from Dublin singer Radie Peat. The reviewer argues that her stark, unornamented delivery strips the quaintness off centuries-old traditional ballads and brings back the rage, heartbreak and political violence inside them.

items.title: Twelve specks of space dust point to a hidden reservoir of heavy water beyond Neptune
items.why: Twelve grains, collected by a high-altitude NASA aircraft sweeping the stratosphere, are being asked to testify about the birth of the solar system. They make a decent case: the outer region seems to have kept its own stock of deuterium-rich water that never mixed inward. Notice how much planetary science now rests on things you need an electron microscope to find.
items.summary: Researchers at NASA's Johnson Space Center and UCLA studied twelve interplanetary dust grains gathered by a high-flying aircraft. In a Science Advances paper they argue the grains show that the region beyond Neptune once held a large, isolated reservoir of heavy water that never blended with the material that formed the inner planets.

items.title: User namespaces plus file capabilities: how container root keeps leaking out
items.why: User namespaces were supposed to give a container a root that is only root at home, and the ensuing decade has been a long list of exceptions. Corbet walks through one more, where file capabilities let a process inside the namespace hand extra privilege to something outside it. A good refresher on why the init-of-the-namespace rules are so fiddly, and why each fix seems to break somebody's container setup.
items.summary: Jonathan Corbet examines a small patch series from Josef Bacik aimed at cases where a process inside a user namespace can raise the privileges of processes outside it, via file capabilities. The article lays out how the first process in a user namespace is treated and where the containment has proved leaky.

items.title: A Dreamcast mod that plays Nintendo 64 cartridges
items.why: Two rival consoles of the late 90s, finally reconciled by someone with a soldering iron and too much free time. The interesting bit is that the Dreamcast's Maple bus peripherals make this sort of thing more plausible than it sounds. It is the kind of gloriously pointless hack the scene exists for.
items.summary: Hackaday covers a build that adds Nintendo 64 cartridge compatibility to a Sega Dreamcast, using an add-on that plugs into the console's peripheral system. The write-up also recalls how unusually forward-looking the Dreamcast was, with a built-in modem and VGA output.

items.title: Christine de Pizan's Epistle of Othea, in gently illustrated miniatures
items.why: Christine de Pizan wrote this around 1400 as a book of advice for a young knight, framed as letters from the goddess Othea, with each lesson pinned to a myth. This fifteenth-century copy illustrates war and legend with an oddly serene hand. Good for a slow scroll, and a reminder that the first professional woman writer in France was handing out career advice to noblemen.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review has a collection of miniatures from a copy of Christine de Pizan's Epistle of Othea made around 1460. The book offers moral guidance to young noblemen through episodes from classical myth, and its pictures of battles and gods are surprisingly calm.

items.title: Wax, the bee-haunted art film that was the first movie streamed on the internet
items.why: In 1993 a handful of university computer labs gathered to watch a film over the network, and of all things it was David Blair's dreamlike science fiction about bees, missiles and television. The Mbone-era context alone is catnip for anyone who remembers multicast being the future. Kali Wallace's column takes the film itself seriously too, which it probably deserves.
items.summary: Reactor's Science Fiction Film Club revisits Wax, or the Discovery of Television Among the Bees, a 1991 experimental film written, directed by and starring David Blair. The column recalls its 1993 screening over the internet to scattered computer labs and digs into its strange story of beekeeping, time and space.

items.title: A retired teacher who has now seen all 18 penguin species
items.why: Every birder has a quest; Lori Fleischmann's took nearly thirty years and several of the planet's least convenient coastlines. Having ticked all eighteen recognised penguin species, she has moved on to subspecies, which is either admirable or a warning. A pleasant read for any solo birder plotting the next impossible list.
items.summary: 10,000 Birds interviews Lori Fleischmann, a retired New York City public school teacher who recently finished a roughly 30-year quest to see every currently recognised penguin species. She talks about why penguins, and about her next goal of tracking down their subspecies.

items.title: The Negro Leagues Baseball Museum in Kansas City
items.why: Kansas City is where the Negro National League was founded in 1920, so the museum sits in exactly the right place, in the old 18th and Vine jazz district. It tells a story of brilliant baseball played in spite of everything. James Earl Jones narrating the introductory film is reason enough to get there early.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura describes this privately funded, nonprofit museum in Kansas City, Missouri, devoted to the teams and players of the Negro Leagues. A self-guided tour takes in photos, artifacts, films and a timeline of baseball alongside African American history, including a museum-only film narrated by James Earl Jones.

items.title: 125,000 years ago, hippos wallowed in lakes where Arabia's desert is now
items.why: The Arabian interior was not always sand: during wetter spells it held big lakes, hippos and people with surprisingly clever hunting kit. The detail to notice is the hint that these hunters may have boosted their weapons with plant poisons. A nice corrective to the idea that deserts are permanent fixtures.
items.summary: Work at a 125,000-year-old site in Saudi Arabia finds that early humans lived beside large lakes teeming with wildlife, hippos included, in what is now desert. Thousands of stone tools and preserved plant remains suggest fairly sophisticated hunting, possibly with weapons treated with toxic plant compounds.

items.title: Sarah Jarosz takes ten years of Undercurrent to Bloomington's Buskirk-Chumley Theater
items.why: Undercurrent is the record that won Jarosz her Grammys, and she has been touring it this autumn as a tenth-anniversary celebration. This stop is Indiana's turn. A decade on, it is a good excuse to go back and notice how much those spare, close-miked songs leave out on purpose.
items.summary: A press release in Indiana University's student paper announces that Sarah Jarosz's '10 Years of Undercurrent' tour is coming to the Buskirk-Chumley Theater in Bloomington. The tour revisits her 2016 album, which won the Grammy for Best Folk Album.

items.title: Yakamys: a 30-kilo rodent from Thailand, 34 million years ago
items.why: Not a dinosaur, but a fresh fossil from Southeast Asia, which is close enough to home for a Penang reader to count. Giant rodents were supposed to be a later invention; this one turns up roughly twice the size of anything else gnawing at the time. The species name honours Princess Sirindhorn, a long-time patron of Thai science.
items.summary: Researchers have described Yakamys sirindhornae from fossils found in Thailand dating to about 34 million years ago. At an estimated 30 kilograms it is about double the size of other rodents known from that period, which pushes the origin of very large rodents much further back than expected.

items.title: NASA spins Mars helicopter rotor blades past the speed of sound
items.why: Ingenuity proved you could fly on Mars; the catch is that air at one percent of Earth's density gives you almost nothing to push against. Going supersonic at the blade tips was long treated as off-limits because of shock losses, so getting roughly 30 percent more lift out of it is a genuine engineering result rather than a press-release flourish.
items.summary: NASA engineers have tested rotor blades for future Mars helicopters with their tips moving faster than sound in thin, Mars-like air. The tests showed about 30 percent more potential lift, which could let later rotorcraft carry heavier instruments and range further than Ingenuity did.

items.title: Are Uranus and Neptune really rock giants? Argon-40 could tell us
items.why: The tidy gas-giant, ice-giant split has been wobbling for a while, and this paper suggests a neat way to settle it: argon-40 comes from the decay of potassium in rock, so how much of it sits in the atmosphere says something about how much rock lies underneath. It is also, quietly, an argument for sending a probe there.
items.summary: A paper led by Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute, in The Planetary Science Journal, proposes measuring argon-40 in the atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune. Because this isotope is produced by radioactive decay in rocky material, its abundance could reveal whether the 'ice giants' are actually dominated by rock deep inside.

items.title: Locking down hibernation for the winter: signing the image the kernel resumes from
items.why: Lockdown has always simply switched hibernation off, because the kernel has no way to know the image it reads back has not been tampered with. Matthew Garrett's patches aim to close that gap so locked-down machines can hibernate again. The interesting part is where the keys live and what the resume path is prepared to trust.
items.summary: LWN covers a patch set from Matthew Garrett that would let hibernation coexist with the kernel's lockdown mode. Today lockdown disables hibernation entirely, since a modified memory image on disk could be used to change the running kernel; the patches add a way to verify the image before resuming from it.

items.title: Reverse-engineering the undocumented next-page prefetcher in Skylake-X
items.why: Intel's optimisation manual says next to nothing about its next-page prefetchers, so someone went and measured one. This is the patient, timing-loop-and-spreadsheet kind of microarchitecture work that tells you how the chip behaves at a page boundary rather than how the marketing says it does.
items.summary: A blog post works out how the next-page prefetcher in Intel's Skylake-X cores behaves, using careful experiments because Intel has documented almost nothing about it since a one-paragraph mention for Ivy Bridge. It looks at what triggers prefetching across a page boundary and in which directions.

items.title: The Robinson projection, the world map that splits the difference
items.why: Every flat map lies; the Robinson projection just lies evenly and politely. Arthur Robinson built it in 1963 for Rand McNally and chose it by eye rather than by formula, which is why it looks right even though it preserves nothing exactly. National Geographic used it for a decade before switching to Winkel tripel.
items.summary: Today's Wikipedia featured picture is a world map drawn in the Robinson projection. Arthur H. Robinson devised it in 1963 as a compromise view of the whole globe for Rand McNally, and the National Geographic Society used it for its world maps from 1988 to 1998.

items.title: Boston wants new historical markers, and asks what deserves a plaque
items.why: A city with more history than wall space is asking residents to nominate sites and stories for new markers. Boston.com is also collecting the ones that probably won't make the official list, which is where the good odd stuff tends to live: the forgotten shop, the near-miss invention, the street that used to be a river.
items.summary: The City of Boston has opened nominations for new historical markers, inviting residents to suggest sites and stories worth commemorating. Boston.com is gathering readers' ideas, including the more unusual ones unlikely to be chosen.

items.title: The Wizard of Oz, read through the four Hippocratic humors
items.why: Four travellers each missing one vital quality is a set-up that practically begs for a medieval medical reading. Lee Weinstein maps Baum's story, and mostly the 1939 film, onto the old theory of blood, phlegm and the two biles. It's a pleasing bit of literary detective work about one of fantasy's founding texts.
items.summary: An essay on File 770 by Lee Weinstein looks at L. Frank Baum's The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, and above all the 1939 MGM film with Judy Garland, in the light of the ancient Hippocratic theory of the four bodily humors.

items.title: The horse made the state: an argument that empires grew from the saddle, not the granary
items.why: The textbook story says farming came first, then surplus grain, then kings. Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene argues the other way round: what made large states possible was moving people and armies fast, from the steppe to the sea. It's a big claim, but a fun one to argue with over coffee.
items.summary: In an Aeon essay, historian Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene argues that the origins of the state lie less in agriculture and stored grain than in transport and mobility, and the conquest that horses and later ships made possible.

items.title: Nyana rooiwalensis: a nearly complete skull from South Africa names a new early sauropodomorph
items.why: A skull dug up near a South African village back in 2018 has finally been worked up and turns out to be something nobody had named. Early sauropodomorphs are where the giant long-necks began, before anyone got enormous, and a near-complete skull is the part palaeontologists almost never get.
items.summary: Sci.News reports a new species of early sauropodomorph dinosaur, named Nyana rooiwalensis, described from a nearly complete skull found in South Africa in 2018. It adds another branch to the crowded family tree of small, early relatives of the later giant sauropods.

items.title: Tethyshadros, Italy's island duck-bill, had a beak as intricate as a bird's
items.why: Island dinosaurs are always a little odd, and this 81-million-year-old hadrosaur from what is now Italy is no exception. The fun part is a correction: the spiky comb once reconstructed at the tip of its snout turns out not to have been there, and the real beak was a more bird-like piece of kit.
items.summary: A new analysis of Tethyshadros insularis, a small duck-billed dinosaur that lived on an island in the ancient Tethys sea, finds its snout tip lacked the row of tooth-like spikes previously proposed. Instead the beak appears to have been as structurally complex as those of modern birds.

items.title: Punch Brothers light up Toronto's Koerner Hall
items.why: Another stop on the Punch Brothers tour, and another reviewer won over. Koerner Hall is a proper acoustic room built for chamber music, which is more or less the genre Chris Thile and company have been smuggling bluegrass instruments into for two decades.
items.summary: The New Classical FM reviews a Punch Brothers concert at Koerner Hall in Toronto, part of the band's current tour. The piece files it under its Scrutiny review series.

items.title: Hanneke Cassel Band and Dallahan share a bill this weekend in Rhode Island
items.why: Hanneke Cassel's Boston-based fiddle band paired with Dallahan, a group that mixes Irish and Scottish tunes with a bit of Hungarian swagger, is about as good a double bill as New England fiddle fans get in November. Worth noting if anyone in the family is near Woonsocket.
items.summary: The Valley Breeze previews a show presented by BRT, the Blackstone River Theatre in Rhode Island, featuring the Hanneke Cassel Band alongside the Celtic group Dallahan this weekend.

items.title: The Empire State Building turns gold as Voyager 1 nears one light-day from Earth
items.why: Launched in 1977 with less computing power than a car key fob, Voyager 1 is about to be a full light-day away, so a command sent at breakfast gets answered the next morning. New York marked it by lighting its most famous tower in the colour of the golden record.
items.summary: NASA's image of the day shows the Empire State Building lit gold on 17 November 2026 to celebrate Voyager 1 approaching one light-day from Earth. No other human-made object has travelled that far.

items.title: Marc Brooker on why your load tests miss the bug: traffic mix
items.why: Brooker takes one sentence from a recent outage report, that lab load tests missed the problem because of the traffic mix they used, and pulls on it. Anyone who has watched a benchmark pass and production fall over will recognise the shape of the argument.
items.summary: A short essay from Marc Brooker arguing that the mix of request types, not just the volume, decides how a large system behaves under load. Synthetic tests that get the mix wrong can sail past latent issues that real traffic triggers.

items.title: A giant 3D-printed Tamagotchi that is really a manga e-reader
items.why: The original Tamagotchi asked you to feed a pixel pet; this one asks you to read. It is a cheerful, slightly absurd hobby build of exactly the kind Hackaday exists for, and a reminder that a good enclosure joke can carry a whole project.
items.summary: Maker Arnov Sharma built a homemade manga reader housed in an oversized 3D-printed shell styled like the classic Tamagotchi. The scaled-up case is big enough to hold a screen suited to reading digital comics.

items.title: Veliki Kalnik Castle, a medieval fort that grows out of a Croatian ridge
items.why: Some castles sit on a hill; this one seems to have been extruded from it. First recorded in the 1240s, it comes with a legend about a fleeing Hungarian king, which is the sort of footnote that makes the climb worth it.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura profiles Veliki Kalnik, a medieval stronghold above the village of Kalnik in northern Croatia. Its towers and walls follow a jagged rocky ridge across several levels, and local legend ties it to King Béla IV taking refuge there.

items.title: A physicist's plan to teach birds songs they have lost
items.why: Birdsong is learned, which means that when a population crashes, whole dialects can quietly go extinct. This Aeon short follows a physicist trying to put lost melodies back into the repertoire, a lovely mix of acoustics and conservation for anyone who birds by ear.
items.summary: An Aeon video about a physicist working to revive bird songs that have faded as populations declined. The project treats song as culture passed between birds, and tries to restore what has been lost.

items.title: How M.C. Escher's prints build impossible mathematical worlds
items.why: Escher famously never passed a maths exam, then spent his career drawing things mathematicians still write papers about. Quanta walks through how his tilings and warped spaces map onto real geometry, which is a pleasant way to spend a coffee.
items.summary: Quanta Magazine looks at the Dutch printmaker M.C. Escher, born in Leeuwarden in 1898, who struggled with school mathematics yet became a favourite of mathematicians. The piece explains the geometry behind his tessellations and impossible spaces.

items.title: Harvard Book Store opens a second shop near Faneuil Hall
items.why: Nur sent this one in, and it is the rare retail story that reads as good news: an independent bookshop expanding rather than closing. The location is the nice touch, the old Yankee Magazine building, which means a New England institution moving into another one's old rooms. Bonus points for the cafe, since browsing is thirsty work.
items.summary: Harvard Book Store, the Cambridge independent, is opening a second location on Union Street near Faneuil Hall this Saturday, complete with a cafe. It is the shop's first Boston outpost since its Newbury Street branch closed in 1994.

items.title: Raleigh's museum opens a 5,000-pound field jacket holding a rare ostrich-like dinosaur from Utah
items.why: Ornithomimids, the long-legged ostrich mimics, are delicate animals and rarely survive as more than scraps, so a block this big is a promising sign. The Raleigh museum does its prep work behind glass, which means visitors get to watch the plaster come off rather than reading about it two years later. Same lab that hosted the Dueling Dinosaurs, so they know how to unwrap a big present.
items.summary: Palaeontologists at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences have begun opening a plaster-wrapped block weighing about 5,000 pounds that contains a rare ostrich-like dinosaur collected in Utah. The work is happening in the museum's public lab, so visitors can watch the fossil emerge.

items.title: Alsasuacaris: a 1.6-millimetre Cretaceous cyclidan that may have ridden on sea reptiles
items.why: Cyclidans are one of palaeontology's odder loose ends, crab-shaped arthropods that are not crabs and whose relationships still start arguments. This one is barely bigger than a sesame seed, and the suggestion that it lived on marine reptiles turns a Maastricht quarry find into a tiny ecology puzzle. Not a dinosaur, but it lived in their oceans.
items.summary: Researchers have described a new species of cyclidan, an extinct group of crab-like arthropods, from a single 1.6-millimetre specimen found in a quarry near Maastricht. They propose that the animal may have lived on the bodies of large marine reptiles.

items.title: FreeBSD's GUS, the safe memory reclamation scheme hiding in the code comments
items.why: Anyone who has lived with RCU knows the interesting part is never the reader fast path but the bookkeeping that decides when memory can be freed. FreeBSD's global unbounded sequences do that job with a different set of trade-offs, and XNU picked it up too, yet it has mostly been documented in comments. A proper write-up for people who already know why lock-free code needs one.
items.summary: A detailed explanation of GUS, FreeBSD's safe memory reclamation mechanism for lock-free data structures, which plays a role similar to Linux's RCU and was later adopted by Apple's XNU kernel. The post walks through the problem it solves and how the scheme works, filling a gap left by documentation that lived mostly in source comments.

items.title: TLAPS-Bench: putting the TLA+ proof system to work on real system specs
items.why: Most people meet TLA+ through the TLC model checker, which is great right up until you ask about more than three nodes and a handful of values. Murat looks at the less travelled road, deductive proofs with TLAPS, and a benchmark built from real specifications. Worth reading for the honest account of where proofs still hurt.
items.summary: Murat Demirbas reviews TLAPS-Bench, a benchmark of real-world system specifications for the TLA+ Proof System. The piece contrasts model checking, which covers only the configurations you give it, with hierarchical deductive proofs that hold for all configurations, and looks at how well proving can be made practical.

items.title: Unkernel: Linux 7.x compiled to a single WebAssembly module, MMU and all
items.why: We have had browser Linux before, mostly as an emulated x86 chugging along. This one compiles the kernel itself to wasm, so the scheduler, memory management and filesystems run as real compiled code and only user programs are emulated. Pure late-90s energy: nobody needed it, someone built it anyway.
items.summary: Hackaday covers Unkernel, a project that builds a recent Linux kernel as one WebAssembly module with its own MMU so it runs in a browser tab at a fair fraction of native speed. Kernel internals such as syscalls, scheduling, memory management and networking are compiled directly, while user programs are emulated.

items.title: An upside-down DreamZzz cauldron becomes the perfect LEGO diving helmet
items.why: The best part usage is the kind that makes you suspect the designers planned it all along. Flipping a big specialised cauldron piece into a brass diving helmet is exactly that sort of trick, and the seabed scene around it is full of treasure for the patient looker.
items.summary: Builder nuhvok_mok has made an undersea LEGO scene with an old-style diver whose helmet is the large cauldron piece from the DreamZzz line, turned upside down. The Brothers Brick highlights the build for its near-perfect part usage.

items.title: Glass Wonders Gallery, a glowing collection in Poland's Karkonosze Mountains
items.why: A small mountain-town museum devoted to glass sounds modest until uranium glass enters the conversation, the faintly radioactive green stuff that glows under ultraviolet light. Karpacz is already a walking town in the Giant Mountains, so this makes a good rainy-afternoon stop.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura profiles the Glass Wonders Gallery in Karpacz, in south-western Poland's Karkonosze Mountains, a gallery of colourful glasswork. Highlights include pieces of rare uranium glass that glow under ultraviolet light.

items.title: Tensegrity robots that squish and roll like slugs, for terrain wheels can't handle
items.why: Wheels have a long and distinguished record of getting stuck on other planets. This design borrows tensegrity, the struts-and-cables trick from architecture, to make a robot that changes shape to squeeze through crevices and over boulders. Early days, but a refreshing change from adding a seventh wheel.
items.summary: Engineers at Colorado State University's Adaptive Robotics Lab describe, in Nature Machine Intelligence, a shape-shifting robot built on tensegrity principles. Its flexible body lets it crawl through jagged, cramped ground that defeats wheeled rovers, which could make it useful for exploring rough alien terrain.

items.title: Checking whether the cosmic microwave background's tiny twist is real
items.why: A slight rotation in the polarisation of the oldest light would be a genuine sign of new physics, which is exactly why everyone suspects the telescopes first. The interesting part here is not a discovery but a way to separate instrument error from sky signal, the unglamorous step that decides whether a hint becomes a result.
items.summary: Researchers at UC San Diego have developed a technique to rule out telescope calibration errors when measuring a possible rotation in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background. If the signal survives, it could point to new physics connected to dark matter or dark energy.

items.title: Homework from 1859: steam engines to the sun and a cow on a tether
items.why: Victorian arithmetic textbooks had a gift for word problems that wander off into the absurd. How long would a train take to reach the sun, and how long a rope gives a cow exactly one acre of grazing? The cow is the classic, a geometry problem that has outlived the book by a century and a half.
items.summary: Futility Closet collects a handful of puzzles from Francis Walkingame's arithmetic textbook of 1859, answers included. They range from a railway journey to the sun to the length of rope that limits a tethered cow to one acre of grass.

items.title: Simulations suggest Webb's 'little red dots' are wrapped-up supermassive primordial stars
items.why: The compact red smudges in early JWST deep fields have been a standing embarrassment for galaxy-formation models, too bright and too small for anyone's comfort. This is one more candidate explanation rather than a verdict, but a simulation that reproduces them is worth a look while the theorists keep arguing.
items.summary: A new set of computer simulations proposes that the tiny, very red objects Webb keeps finding in the young universe are remnants of enormous primordial stars buried inside thick envelopes of gas. The authors argue this fits the dots' odd colours and compact sizes better than earlier ideas.

items.title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer timed Io and showed that light takes time to travel
items.why: The original latency measurement: a moon used as a clock, and a prediction that it would be ten minutes late. Rømer put his neck out in front of the Paris academy with a specific date, which is still the best way to do science, and the anniversary is a nice excuse to retell it.
items.summary: In 1676 the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer, working at the Paris Observatory, predicted that Io would emerge from Jupiter's shadow later than the tables said, because the light had farther to travel. He was right, and the result overturned the old belief that light arrives instantly.

items.title: BTrDB: a copy-on-write, versioned k-ary tree for trillions of time-series points, via The Morning Paper
items.why: A storage paper where the data structure does the heavy lifting: time-partitioned, copy-on-write and version-annotated, so statistical queries over billions of points come back in a couple of hundred milliseconds. Colyer's write-up skips the marketing and goes straight to why the tree is shaped the way it is.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer walks through the 2016 Anderson and Culler paper on BTrDB, a time-series database built for high-rate grid sensors. A few thousand lines of Go stored 2.1 trillion points in production on a small cluster, with fast aggregate queries thanks to precomputed statistics in a versioned tree.

items.title: Vx32: user-level sandboxing on x86 with segments and binary translation (2008)
items.why: Back when x86 segmentation still worked, Bryan Ford and Russ Cox used it to fence in untrusted code's data accesses and a lightweight translator to keep its control flow honest, no kernel module required. It's a neat reminder of what the 32-bit architecture let you get away with, and it later underpinned running Plan 9 kernels in user space.
